title: S&P 500 Sets New Record; Stock Futures Remain Steady in Live CNBC Updates
body:
U.S. equity futures barely shifted Wednesday morning after the S&P 500 closed Tuesday at a fresh all‑time high, buoyed by a surge in technology shares that lifted the benchmark to a record‑breaking level. The rally, driven chiefly by heavyweight chipmakers and cloud‑computing firms, underscored the market’s continued appetite for growth‑oriented stocks even as investors remain wary of lingering inflation pressures and an uncertain monetary‑policy outlook.

The S&P 500’s ascent to a new intraday peak and its subsequent record close were anchored by a string of strong earnings reports and upbeat guidance from several marquee tech companies. Nvidia, whose earnings beat expectations and forecast robust demand for artificial‑intelligence chips, surged more than 8% in after‑hours trading, while Microsoft and Alphabet each posted double‑digit gains after unveiling expanded cloud‑service contracts. The broader tech sector, represented by the Nasdaq‑100, outperformed the broader market, posting a 2.3% rise that helped offset weakness in more cyclical segments such as energy and industrials.

Analysts attribute the market’s resilience to a combination of factors. First, the latest data on consumer prices showed a modest slowdown in inflation, prompting speculation that the Federal Reserve may adopt a more measured approach to rate hikes in the coming months. Second, corporate earnings season remains in its early stages, and the upbeat results from high‑profile tech firms have reinforced expectations that profit growth can continue despite a tighter monetary environment. “The technology rally is a clear signal that investors are betting on the long‑term secular growth of AI and cloud infrastructure, rather than getting caught up in short‑term rate‑policy concerns,” said Laura Chen, senior market strategist at Meridian Capital.

Nevertheless, the optimism is not universal. Energy stocks lagged, with oil prices slipping amid reports of oversupply and weaker demand forecasts, dragging down the energy‑heavy S&P 500 Energy Index. Meanwhile, some investors expressed caution over the valuation levels in the tech sector, which now trade at price‑to‑earnings multiples that are among the highest in the index’s history. “While the earnings beat is encouraging, the market is pricing in very aggressive growth assumptions. Any slowdown in AI spending or a surprise rate hike could trigger a sharp correction,” warned James O’Leary, chief economist at Global Insight.

Futures for the Dow Jones Industrial Average and the Nasdaq Composite mirrored the S&P’s modest movement, indicating that the broader market is likely to open with limited volatility. The modest shift in futures suggests that traders are digesting the day’s gains rather than chasing further upside, a pattern that could hint at a short‑term consolidation phase. Volume on the New York Stock Exchange remained robust, however, signaling that participation remains broad and that the record close was not the result of a narrow, speculative rally.

Looking ahead, market participants will be closely watching upcoming data releases, including the consumer confidence index and the upcoming jobs report, which could provide fresh clues about the health of the U.S. economy and the trajectory of monetary policy. In addition, the next wave of earnings from mid‑cap technology firms and semiconductor manufacturers will test whether the current enthusiasm for AI‑driven growth can be sustained. If the macro environment remains supportive and earnings continue to beat expectations, the S&P 500 could extend its record run; otherwise, a pullback may emerge as investors reassess risk in the face of potential policy tightening.
